title: Numbers, time and dates
goal: Say numbers, times, days, months and dates the Malaysian way — including the half-hour, which Malay says just like English but Indonesian says the other way round, so it has made plenty of people an hour late.
bekal: say numbers, prices and phone numbers the Malaysian way
tell the time without getting lost in *setengah* (half)
name the days and months, several of which come straight from English

dialogs.title: Dialogue — An appointment that nearly went wrong
dialogs.intro: Aina knocks on Sarah's door. There's an extra class tomorrow, and they need to be sure about the time.

lines.speaker: Aina:
lines.text: Sarah, esok ada kelas tambahan. Pukul tiga setengah petang.
lines.id: Sarah, there's an extra class tomorrow. At half past three in the afternoon.
lines.literal: Sarah, tomorrow there-is class extra. o'clock three half afternoon.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Pukul tiga setengah? Maksudnya pukul setengah tiga?
lines.id: Three-half? You mean half past two?
lines.literal: o'clock three half? its-meaning o'clock half three?

lines.speaker: Aina:
lines.text: Eh, tak. Tiga setengah tu 3.30. Lepas tiga, sebelum empat.
lines.id: Oh, no. Three-half is 3:30. After three, before four.
lines.literal: eh, no. three half that 3.30. past three, before four.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Ya Allah. Kat Indonesia "setengah empat" tu 3.30. Kami kira ke depan.
lines.id: Oh my God. In Indonesia "half four" is 3:30. We count forward.
lines.literal: O God. at Indonesia "half four" that 3.30. we count to front.

lines.speaker: Aina:
lines.text: Wah, bahaya tu. Kalau macam tu, sebut je nombor: tiga tiga puluh.
lines.id: Wow, that's dangerous. In that case, just say the numbers: three thirty.
lines.literal: wow, danger that. if like that, say just number: three three-ten.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Setuju. Kelas tu hari apa? Khamis ke Jumaat?
lines.id: Agreed. What day is the class? Thursday or Friday?
lines.literal: agree. class that day what? Thursday or Friday?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.id: Mac? Not Mac like the fast food?

lines.speaker: Aina:
lines.text: Hahaha! Mac tu bulan ketiga. March. Kat Indonesia Maret kan?
lines.id: Hahaha! Mac is the third month. March. In Indonesia it's Maret, right?
lines.literal: hahaha! Mac that month third. March. at Indonesia Maret right?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Betul. Ada berapa lagi bulan yang lain namanya?
lines.id: Right. How many other months have different names?
lines.literal: right. there-is how-many more month that different its-name?

lines.speaker: Aina:
lines.text: Tiga je: Mac, Jun, Julai, Ogos. Eh, empat.
lines.id: Just three: Mac, Jun, Julai, Ogos. Oh, four.
lines.literal: three only: Mac, Jun, Julai, Ogos. eh, four.

notes: **Good news for English speakers:** Malay says the half-hour in English order. *Pukul tiga setengah* is literally "o'clock three half" = three-thirty, 3:30. The trap is Indonesian (and Dutch and German), which counts **forward**: *setengah empat*, "half four", is half-way **to** four = 3:30. And British "half four" means 4:30! If you've learned Indonesian, don't translate word for word, or you'll be a full hour off.

**Haribulan** ("day-month", written as one word) is the Malaysian word for **date** when you say the day of the month. *Lima belas haribulan* = the fifteenth. *Tarikh* also means date, but it's used more in writing and on forms: *Tarikh lahir* = date of birth.

**Ke** in the middle of a question means **or**: *Khamis ke Jumaat?* = "Thursday or Friday?" This is different from the question *ke* at the end of a sentence (unit 1) and from *ke* meaning "to (a place)". Three different *ke*, told apart by position.
**Lepas** = past, after. *Lepas tiga* = past three. It also means "after (doing)": *lepas makan* = after eating.
**Kira** = to count, to calculate. *Kami kira ke depan* = we count forward. ⚠️ Don't confuse it with *kira-kira* (= about, roughly).

grammars.title: Telling the time
body: The pattern: **pukul** (o'clock) + number + extra. Malay uses *jam* (hour) mainly for **a length of time** (*tiga jam* = three hours) and **pukul** for **a point in time** (*pukul tiga* = three o'clock).
after: **Suku** means quarter. *Pukul tiga suku* = 3:15. *Kurang* means "less": *empat kurang suku* = four less a quarter = 3:45. Don't confuse *suku* with *suku* meaning "tribe"; same word, and context tells them apart.
**Minit** = minute (from English), **saat** = second — and also "moment". Clock hands are *jarum* (needles).

grammars.title: Numbers
body: Malay numbers are completely regular: learn one to ten and the rest builds itself — *belas* = -teen, *puluh* = tens, *ratus* = hundreds, *ribu* = thousands, and *se-* = one.

Note
rows: satu, dua, tiga, empat, lima, enam, tujuh

after: Numbers combine just as you'd expect: *dua puluh lima* = 25, *lapan belas* = 18, *lapan puluh* = 80, *seratus dua puluh* = 120. Ordinals take *ke-*: *ketiga* = third, *kelapan* = eighth (except *pertama* = first).

**Decimal point, not comma.** Malaysia follows the English convention: *RM12.50* (read *dua belas ringgit lima puluh sen*), *1,000* for a thousand — exactly as in English. ⚠️ Indonesia does the opposite (Rp12.500), so watch out if you read Indonesian prices.

blocks.text: Most Malay day names come from Arabic. Learn the seven as a set:

**Ahad** is Sunday. The word *minggu* means **week** (a seven-day period) — *minggu depan* (next week), *dua minggu lagi* (in two weeks) — but it isn't a day name in Malaysia. (Indonesians call Sunday *Minggu*; Malaysians will understand it, but it marks you out at once.)
The month names come from English, so they're easy for you — just note the Malay spelling:

Aina miscounts in the dialogue: there are five that differ from Indonesian, not four — **Disember** with an *i* is easy to miss. For you, the ones to watch are the spellings *Mac*, *Jun*, *Julai*, *Ogos* and *Disember*. When you fill in a form in Malaysia, these are the spellings used.

**Lepas** is the word for "last" with past time: *minggu lepas*, *bulan lepas*, *tahun lepas*. The form *yang lalu* is also correct and used in formal writing, but in conversation it's almost always *lepas*.

blocks.title: Writing dates
items: **The order is day-month-year**, as in British English: *15 Mac 2026*.
⚠️ Don't use the American order (*03/15/2026*) — it isn't used in Malaysia and will be misread.
*Tarikh lahir* = date of birth. *Tarikh tamat tempoh* = expiry date (on food and cards).
Years are read as a whole number: *dua ribu dua puluh enam* (two thousand twenty-six), never split into "twenty twenty-six".

exercises.prompt: Write these times in Malay (use *setengah* and *suku* where you can).
Fill in the right Malay day or month.
items: Hari cuti hujung minggu ialah Sabtu dan ____.
The class is on Thursday, the fifteenth of March.
My phone number is zero one two, three four five.
Last month I went to Singapore.
Tomorrow at eight in the morning.

answers: pukul tujuh — pukul sembilan suku — pukul dua setengah — pukul enam kurang suku — pukul dua belas tengah hari — pukul lapan setengah malam
Khamis — Jumaat — Isnin — Ahad — Mac — Ogos

Sekarang pukul tiga setengah. — Kelas tu hari Khamis, lima belas haribulan Mac. — Nombor telefon saya kosong satu dua, tiga empat lima. — Saya datang semalam. — Bulan lepas saya ke Singapura. — Esok pukul lapan pagi.
